## REVIEW

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

## Analysis of the current state of sewage sludge treatment from the perspective of current European directives

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Jozef Salva , Michal Sečkár , Marián Schwarz , Dagmar Samešová , Martina Mordáčová , Juraj Poništ 1 1 1 1 1 1* and Darina Veverková 2

## Abstract

Due to its produced quantity, sewage sludge is a serious environmental problem not only in Slovakia, but also on a global scale. The submitted study deals with the current state of sewage sludge treatment with a focus on assessing the advantages and disadvantages of selected technologies. The main objective of the review study is to evaluate the advantages and limitations of individual sewage sludge processing technologies. Based on the evaluation of the advantages and limitations, another objective of the study was to determine the most suitable, less suitable, or unsuitable technologies for sewage sludge processing. Another objective of the study was to evaluate innovative technologies (not only commonly used ones). The purpose of this objective was to monitor the most current trends in sewage sludge processing technologies and, by evaluating them, to expand knowledge in this scientific field. The presented analysis of sewage sludge treatment was carried out in accordance with current European directives. The main novelty of the review study is a comprehensive assessment of sludge processing technologies with a focus on their main advantages and limitations. Another novelty is the focus of the study on innovative methods of sewage sludge processing. As part of the analysis, the evaluated sludge treatment technologies were divided into three categories: conventional, alternative, and innovative. As a conventional method, composting is currently the dominant method of sewage sludge management in the Slovak Republic. Mono-incineration, which is one of the conventional methods, allows for an effective reduction of the volume of sewage sludge while removing all unwanted hazardous components at the same time. However, this sludge treatment technology causes simultaneously the loss of most of the valuable nutrients, contained in sewage sludge. Pyrolysis and gasification as alternative technologies are effective in terms of removing hazardous components, but they are complex technologies, and their economic viability depends on their ability to maximise efficiency and produce high-value energy carriers. Hydrothermal liquefaction has a major advantage over all other thermal sewage sludge treatment processes because it does not require sludge drying. Innovative methods of sewage sludge treatment such as bio-electrochemical system, supercritical water oxidation, and biodiesel production require a more detailed examination by the scientific community to implement these methods in practice due to the lack of information from operational experiments. Given the extensiveness of the sludge treatment issue, we plan to address the economic aspect of the technologies in a separate study in the future.

Keywords Sludge, biogas, Process strategies, Innovative technologies, energy, Wastewater treatment plant, European directives

## Introduction

Sludge  is  increasingly  a  key  problem  in  municipal  and industrial wastewater treatment. It is generated as waste or a by-product of wastewater treatment processes, and the  handling  and  disposal  of  this  waste  is  complex  and challenging [1]. Sludge from wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs)  is  an  important  by-product  that  contains important  nutrients  and  organic  substances.  Sewage sludge is a by-product of wastewater treatment. It is rich in  nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K), but also contains harmful substances, including heavy metals and associated microorganisms [2, 3]. Sewage sludge is a by-product of the wastewater treatment process, which separates liquid and solid components [4].

The opinion of the European Committee of the Regions on the amendment of the Revision of the Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive C/2023/250 states that member  states  will  take  the  necessary  measures  to  ensure that  sludge  management  methods  are  in  accordance with  the  waste  management  hierarchy,  in  the  Article  4 of  the  Directive  2008/98/EC.  Such  methods  maximise the  prevention  of  wasting  the  sources,  reuse,  recovery and  recycling  of  sources,  and  minimise  adverse  effects on the environment. The Evaluation Report on Council Directive 86/278/EEC on the protection of the environment and soil when sewage sludge is used in agriculture was the source of data for this study. The Water Research Institute  is  commissioned to collect, verify, process and evaluate data on sludge produced from municipal wastewater  treatment  plants  and  methods  of  their  management. This data and information shall be published on an annual basis.

Depending  on  where  the  sewage  sludge  comes  from, it is divided into primary and secondary sludge. Primary sludge  contains  settling  substances  contained  in  wastewater (sludge from primary settling tanks). It usually has a granular structure, and dry matter ranges from 2 to 50 g/l. (the amount of solid component per total volume of the  mixture).  Secondary  sludge  (excess)  is  formed  by  a mixture of microorganisms and sedimentable substances from  the  biological  stage  of  the  wastewater  treatment plants.  This  sludge  is  removed  from  the  settling  tanks, its  coexistence  is  flaky,  and  the  composition  affects  the method of  treatment  and  the  supplied  wastewater.  Primary and secondary sludge is referred to as crude. Crude sludge  is  still  microbially  active,  it  may  contain  pathogenic microorganisms, the total content of organic substances  in  the  dry  matter  is  around  70%.  Stabilisation breaks down degradable organic substances, sludge can be  pumped  out  and  is  considered  harmless  to  health. Sludge stabilisation is the name for the process by which we adjust the final properties of the sludge so that spontaneous decomposition no longer occurs [5]. The aerobic sludge stabilisation process is the most commonly used, in treatment plants of different sizes.

In most cases, it is a biochemical process of reducing the  content  of  the  residue  of  easily  degradable  organic substances and thus the total concentration of the organic component in the sludge. Determining the sludge stability criterion is not easy. In normal operating practice,  the  limit  of  stability  of  the  sludge  was  considered to be 50% of the organic component, determined as the loss  by  annealing.  Stabilised  sludge  must  not  decompose  spontaneously,  it  must  not  burden  the  surroundings  with  odours.  Simultaneously  with  the  stabilisation of the sludge, the content of pathogenic microorganisms decreases, too, and the method of sludge stabilisation can also be a method of sludge sanitation [5].

The management of sewage sludge processing in Slovakia  (Table  1)  mainly  includes  application  to  agricultural land;  application  to  forest  land;  composting  and  other recovery; energy recovery; incineration or landfilling.

Land application of sewage sludge is one of the important disposal alternatives [3]. Application of waste materials  to  agricultural  land  presents  an  opportunity  for recovery of essential plant nutrients. Many waste products  contain  concentrations  of  plant  nutrient  elements sufficient to produce an agriculturally significant growth response [6]. The diverse composition of sewage sludge from different  wastewater  treatment  plants  and  its  seasonal variations require analysis of the chemical composition before its application to soil [3].

Forest  sludge  application  offers  many  advantages.  Its potential health risk is much lower than that of agricultural application, since forest products from berries and mushrooms to game contribute insignificantly to human nutrition, and forest soils and vegetation are often more amenable  to  sludge  application.  Given  the  perennial stands  with  extensive  roots,  year-round  application  is possible, weather permitting [7].

Composting is a complicated process aimed at destruction  of  pathogenic  organisms;  stabilisation  of  organic matter,  ripening;  drying  of  the  sludge;  production  of material which can be environment ally used or sold [8]. Composting is a widespread method of treating organic solid  waste  (Bari  and  Koenig,  2001).  Its  performance  is influenced by a number of factors, including the ratio of components  in  the  mixture,  aeration  intensity,  oxygen consumption rate, compost recycling, moisture level, pH value, C/N ratio, and others [9]

The  composting  process  is  used  for  sludge  treatment and the transformation of complex biological waste into a stabilised product that can serve as an organic fertilizer and  a  value-added  material.  Composting  occurs  under aerobic conditions, where micro-aeration enhances the hydrolysis of complex substances into simpler

The composting process consists of three stages, classified  based  on  temperature  progression.  In  the  first stage,  mesophilic  microorganisms  thrive,  causing  a  rise in  system  temperature.  As  the  temperature  continues to  increase,  the  second  stage  begins,  characterised  by the activation  of thermophilic  microorganisms.  During this phase, most pathogens are eliminated due to the high-temperature  conditions.  The  final  stage,  known  as the  maturation  phase,  involves  a  gradual  temperature decrease and the reactivation of the mesophilic microbial population [10].

Energy  recovery  from  sludge  is  regarded  as  the  most attractive  methods  for  utilising  the  increasing  quantity of sludge for eliminating volatile organic matter and reducing  waste  volume  with  possibility  of  recovering nutrients  and/or  metals.  Most  of  these  energy  recovery technologies  are  not  new  as  they  have  been  developed commercially for other fuel types, however differences in the  physical  and  chemical  properties  of  sludge  presents unique technical challenges which influences the energy recovery process and reactions [11].

Current  sludge  to  landfill  methods  generally  involve mixing  the  concentrated  sludge  with  other  solid  waste in municipal landfills. However, stricter waste disposal legislation and higher landfill taxes are forcing the water industry to look for more efficient disposal strategies. Landfill operators are also increasingly reluctant to accept sludge material in the slurry state because of construction  difficulties  and  the  potential  for  instability  of the landfill slopes [13].

According  to  the  statistics of the Water  Research Institute, approximately 50,000 to 60,000 tonnes (in dry matter) of sludge has been produced annually at Slovak municipal  wastewater  treatment  plants  for  the  last  20 years.

According  to  the  latest  Assessment  Report,  the  predominant  method  of  sludge  stabilisation  in  the  Slovak Republic  is  aerobic  stabilisation,  which  is  used  by  74% of  WWTPs. To a large extent, this stabilisation method is  practised  in  WWTPs  up  to  10,000  PE.  As  a  result, the  production  of  aerobically  stabilised  sludge  is  only at the level of about 24% of the total sludge production. Approximately  26%  of  the  total  number  of  wastewater treatment  plants  use  anaerobic  stabilisation,  of  which part (about 3% of the total number of wastewater treatment  plants  in  the  Slovak  Republic)  uses  Imhoff  tanks. The  mass  fraction of anaerobically stabilised sludge accounts for approximately 76% of the total sludge production  of  the  Slovak  Republic. Therefore, the technologies used to treat sewage sludge must be chosen with an emphasis on the ability to recycle  the  required  components  while  effectively  removing potentially  hazardous  substances  for  the  environment and human health. Currently, there are several methods by which sewage sludge can be recovered or disposed of. Sewage sludge treatment is still a very current topic and requires a comprehensive view in the scientific field.

Sewage sludge utilisation is a critical aspect of wastewater  treatment,  with  various  methods  being  established  worldwide.  Figure  1  shows  an  analysis  examines the trends in these methods from 2011 to 2022, focusing on  agricultural  use,  composting,  landfilling,  incineration, and other unspecified methods according to Eurostat data. The data include reports from EU-27 countries, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland, United Kingdom, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia,  Albania,  Serbia,  and  Türkiye,  respectively [19].

Fig. 1 Sewage sludge treatment methods in selected countries

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

The agricultural  application  of  sewage  sludge  was  the predominant  utilisation  method  in  the  early  years  of the observed  period.  However,  fluctuations  occurred between  2011  and  2018,  followed  by  a  sharp  decline from 2019 onward. By 2022, the volume of sludge used in  agriculture  had  decreased  significantly,  likely  due  to stricter EU regulations on contaminants in sludge applied to farmland. Composting remained relatively stable over the  years,  with  a  slight  peak  around  2020,  indicating  a temporary increase in composting efforts. However, the overall trend does not suggest significant growth, implying  that  composting  has  not  emerged  as  a  dominant alternative. Landfilling exhibited a clear downward trend, with  volumes  steadily  decreasing  over  time.  A  particularly  sharp  decline  after  2019  likely  reflects  EU  policies aimed  at  reducing  landfill  dependency  and  promoting more sustainable waste management practices. Incineration  increased  from  2011  to  2018,  indicating  a  growing preference for thermal treatment of sewage sludge. However,  in  2022,  a  steep  drop  in  incineration  volumes  was observed.  This  may  be  linked  to  changing  regulations, increased  energy  costs,  or  shifts  towards  more  sustainable utilisation methods. The category of other disposal methods  remained  relatively  stable,  with  minor  fluctuations.  Unlike  other  categories,  it  did  not  exhibit  any dramatic  increases  or  decreases,  suggesting  that  these methods  have  maintained  a  consistent  role  in  sewage sludge treatment management.

The  main  objective  of  the  review  study  is  to  evaluate  the  advantages  and  limitations  of  individual  sewage sludge processing technologies. Based on the evaluation of  the  advantages  and  limitations,  another  objective  of the  study  was  to  determine  the  most  suitable,  less  suitable,  or  unsuitable  technologies  for  sewage  sludge  processing.  Another  objective  of  the  study  was  to  evaluate innovative technologies (not only commonly used ones). The  purpose  of  this  objective  was  to  monitor  the  most current  trends  in  sewage  sludge  processing  technologies  and,  by  evaluating  them,  to  expand  knowledge  in this  scientific  field.  In  addition  to  the  above,  the  objective of the presented review study is to provide a tool for decision-making  when  choosing  a  suitable  technology for  future  sewage  sludge  processing  operations.  Only  a comprehensive study can help in choosing the appropriate technology for processing this type of waste in a specific situation. The analysis of the current state of sewage sludge processing was prepared in accordance with European directives.

## Characteristics of sludge from municipal wastewater treatment plants

According to Act 442/2002 (on public water supply and public  sewerage  systems  and  on  amendments  to  Act

No.  276/2001  Coll.  on  regulation  in  network  sectors), public sewerage is understood as an operationally independent set of objects and facilities serving public needs for the  collective discharge  of  municipal  wastewater [20].  According  to  Act  364/2004  (Act  on  Water  and  on amendments to Act of the Slovak National Council No. 372/1990  Coll.  on  offences,  as  amended  (Water  Act)), municipal wastewater is water from residential areas containing predominantly sewage wastewater; it may contain industrial wastewater, infiltrated water and, in the case of a  unified sewer network or a semi-separated sewer network, also water from surface runoff [21]. It follows from the above that, under certain conditions, it is possible to discharge  industrial  wastewater  through  the  sewerage network with sewage. However, in our study, we focus on the processing of paper sludge exclusively from municipal sewage. Depending on factors such as the development and  size  of  settlements,  industrial  activities,  population characteristics,  and  sewage  services,  sewage  sludge  can contain  several  toxic  substances,  such  as  heavy  metals. Therefore, their presence must be analysed, since some of these metals are essential in agriculture (such as Zn and Cu). At higher concentrations, metals such as nickel and cadmium can have toxic effects in the soil, and the low mobility of such metals increases their concentration in the  soil.  Heavy  metals  (i.e.  As,  Cr,  Hg,  Mo,  Pb,  and  Se) affect  human  and  animal  health,  plant  growth  [22].  An important aspect related to the beneficial or toxic effects of  heavy  metals  contained  in  sewage  sludge  is  the  pH value, since it affects their solubility. In particular, acidic media  can  increase  the  solubility  of  heavy  metals  and make them dynamically toxic; therefore, there may be a high risk associated with the acidic pH range. In case of pharmaceutical  products,  such  as  disinfectants,  cleaning products, pesticides, dyes, paints, preservatives, food additives, personal care products, and organic pollutants, concerns increased due to the public health risk [23]. The pathogens  present  in  sewage  sludge  come  from  human excrement and are directly related to the diet and health state of the population. They can also come from animal sources  whose  excrement  is  discharged  into  the  sewerage system (e.g. dog and cat faeces) or via carriers in the sewers,  especially  rodents  [24].  These  microorganisms, including faecal coliforms, Escherichia coli , Campylobacter and Salmonella sp. , and parasites or viruses pose a risk to human health. Their presence is high in sewage sludge, especially  in  countries  with  low  and  medium  economic level  of  populations  [25,  26].  Despite  the  many  benefits of using sewage sludge in soil, there are still many issues that need to be addressed [27].

About 50 to 80% of the original wastewater pollution is concentrated  in  sludge.  These  substances,  such  as phosphorus, nitrogen and potassium, are important for

the  circular  economy.  The  possibility  of  returning  these substances to the soil could contribute to more sustainable  agricultural  production.  However,  in  addition  to their beneficial composition in terms of nutrient content, it  is  important that sewage sludge can also contain several  harmful  substances  (e.g.  pathogens,  medicaments, microplastics,  heavy  metals,  etc.).  According  to  study [28]  the  range  of  major  nutrients  from  eight  studied WWTPs ranges for N 20,593 ± 2265-60,031 ± 6603 mg/ kg; for P 10,663 ± 521-26,726 ± 1098 mg/kg; for K 4730 ± 198-8102  ± 315  mg/kg.  [28].  Typical  composition  of sludge from municipal WWTPs is shown in Table 2.

## Sewage sludge storage

Sludge can be stored under specific conditions to ensure environmental  protection  and  compliance  with  regulations. In the European Union, the storage of sludge is primarily governed by the Sewage Sludge Directive (86/278/ EEC) and other related regulations (EU Directive 86/278/ EEC on Sewage Sludge. This directive regulates the use of  sludge  in  agriculture  and  includes  provisions  for  its storage to prevent risks to human health, soil, and water. According to the directive:

Storage must be managed safely: Sludge must be stored in  a  way  that  prevents  environmental  contamination, particularly to water sources. Time limits and conditions may apply: Some member states impose specific requirements  on  the  duration  and  location  of  sludge  storage. Quality  control:  Stored  sludge  must  comply  with  heavy metal  limits  and  pathogen  reduction  measures  before application  to  land.  National  regulations:  EU  countries may  impose  stricter  storage  rules  under  their  environmental laws.

Beyond Directive 86/278/EEC, the Industrial Emissions Directive (2010/75/EU) and the Waste Framework Directive  (2008/98/EC)  also  apply  to  sludge  storage  in  cases involving industrial waste or landfill regulations [14].

## Identification of sewage sludge management methods

Each study has a separate treatment distribution key, but within  our  methodology,  we  decided  to  divide  sewage sludge treatment technologies into conventional, alternative,  and innovative methods. Thus, as is apparent from the foregoing information, the basic treatment of sewage sludge is to stabilise  it  in  order  not  to  cause  damage  to the environment and not to cause difficulties when being handled. However, the term stabilisation is not precisely defined by legislation and there is no universal criterion for assessing the stability of sludge.

The  goal  of  sludge  stabilisation  is  to  reduce  organic matter and thus reduce odour, destroy pathogenic organisms,  improve  drainage  and  reduce  the  volume  and weight  of  sludge.  In  general,  sludge  stabilisation  technologies can be divided into anaerobic and aerobic. Each of  these  methods  has  its  advantages  and  disadvantages. Compared  to  aerobic  stabilisation  of  sludge,  anaerobic stabilisation  generally  has  a  lower  energy  performance, but  it  is  more  investment-intensive  and  is  not  suitable for smaller wastewater treatment plants, i.e. &lt; 35,000 PE [29].  Conventional,  alternative,  and  innovative  methods of sewage sludge treatment is presented in Table 3.

Bio-electrochemical system  (BES) is considered as microbial  fuel  cell  (MFC)  that  simultaneously  generates bioenergy and treats wastewater or other biological waste.  In  this  process,  electroactive  microorganisms  on the anode break down organic matter, releasing protons and electrons. These charged particles then travel to the cathode via a proton exchange membrane and an electrical circuit, where they interact with an electron acceptor to produce electricity [62]. So far, only laboratory experiments are being conducted, as use has several challenges [63].

(SCWO) efficiently and environmentally friendly degrades organic compounds using an excess of oxidant [64, 65]. SCWO requires an excess of oxidant to enhance contact  with  organic  compounds,  which  significantly drives  up  operating  costs.  In  contrast,  SCWG  demands very high temperatures up to 1 027 K for complete gasification, leading to high capital expenses due to the harsh reaction  conditions.  Chematur  Engineering  AB  (CEAB Corp.)  of  Sweden  constructed  Europe's  first  pilot-scale plant  for  sewage  sludge  treatment,  designed  to  process 7    m 3 /h.  Since  then,  numerous  pilot  facilities  have  been built and operated across Europe, North America, China, and  Russia,  handling  domestic  and  industrial  sludge  as well as hazardous industrial waste. For instance, the Harlingen Wastewater Treatment Plant in Texas operated a pilot-scale SCWO unit for sludge treatment, confirming the  method's  viability.  Additionally,  a  full-scale  SCWO plant near Tianjin, China, has been successfully treating sludge at a wastewater treatment facility for the past 10 years [57].

Municipal  sewage  sludge  is  increasingly  recognised worldwide as a valuable lipid feedstock for biodiesel production.  This  is  because  the  sludge  naturally  contains high levels of lipids that are directly adsorbed to it. These lipids provide a significant source of energy, including triglycerides,  diglycerides,  monoglycerides,  phospholipids, and free fatty acids from oils and fats. In addition, microorganisms consume organic and inorganic compounds as sources of energy, carbon, and nutrients during wastewater treatment. The cell membranes of these microorganisms-composed primarily of phospholipids-make up a large portion of the sewage sludge, accounting for about 24% to 25% of the cell's dry matter and providing approximately  7%  of  the  oil  from  the  dried  secondary  sludge. Additional studies have found that up to 36.8% by weight of  the  dry  sludge  consists  of  fatty  acids  and  steroids, and  since  the  fatty  acids  are  predominantly  in  the  C10 to  C18 range, they are suitable for biodiesel production [66]. Although sewage sludge is readily available, its use in  biofuel  production is limited by several issues. These include costly pre-treatment processes, the requirement for  significant  amounts  of  organic  solvents  during  lipid extraction, and the need to maintain product quality in line with established standards [67].

In  Slovakia,  but  also  in  other  countries  of  the  world, waste  management  methods  are  carried  out  that  are not  suitable  from  an  environmental  point  of  view.  The aim of this study was to provide an overview of methods for  treatment of sewage sludge, the amount of which is growing worldwide. The methods were divided into the categories:  conventional  (commonly  used),  alternative (less used) and innovative (used on pilot basis or no use at all).

## Material and methods

In our study, methods for the treatment of WWTP sludge are divided into conventional, alternative and innovative. In our study, we include the methods that are commonly used and economically available in Slovakia to the conventional  ones.  Alternative  technologies  are  the  technologies used to a lesser extent in Slovakia, but are still economically and technologically available and proven in practice.

Innovative methods are not used at all in Slovakia and are  still  less  economically  available,  but  from  the  environmental  point  of  view  they  have  many  advantages. The comparison of sewage sludge treatment methods is focused on assessing the advantages, but also the limiting factors in the use of individual procedures. Overall, the following factors were used as evaluation criteria: financial  cost,  environmental  factors,  energy  consumption, presence of hazardous substances and time consumption. This is because the new BREF documents (Best available techniques References documents) came into force during this period. For this reason, it is possible to assume a larger range of publications focused on the issue of sludge treatment.

The  economic  aspect  is  an  important  criterion  for evaluating  sludge  treatment  technology.  In  our  study, less attention was paid to this aspect, because we focused more on criteria such as emission production, equipment life in the technology, hygiene risks, and the generation of difficult-to-use waste from the technology.

Innovative methods were searched using the databases webofscience.com and scopus.com. The search was conducted by entering a large number of keywords regarding treatment of sewage sludge and reading an enormous number of publications from the aforementioned databases.

## Results and discussion

The division, description, and assessment of the methods, based on the above-mentioned criteria, are in Table 4.

Based on the processed References, the most suitable methods for the sewage sludge treatment are:

- -the  most  optimal  method  in  the  combination  of removing  hazardous  substances  is  mono-incineration;
- -alternative thermal processes (pyrolysis and gasification);
- -in all cases, they are the thermal methods that are the most effective in terms of the destruction of hazardous substances;
- -pyrolysis  and  gasification  due  to  high  temperatures remove hazardous substances effectively. The output is a solid carbon residue, from which phosphorus can be recycled. However, it is necessary to add that these technologies are still in the research stage;
- -innovative methods  seem  to  be  environmentally friendly, but they are not used in practice to a greater extent. The high cost of construction and operation is perceived as a negative factor of these methods. It is difficult to estimate how these processes, when being in full operation mode, will affect the environment in the future.

From the perspective of the expected future trends in sewage sludge management, we expect a trend of gradual tightening of the parameters of sewage sludge in terms of hazardous substances, which will disqualify its use in soil applications  and,  on  the  contrary,  prefer  thermal  methods  of  sewage  sludge  management.  Nowadays,  some EU  countries  are  introducing  a  legislative  obligation  to recover phosphorus from sewage sludge. Therefore, it is possible to assume that such an obligation will be implemented in the Slovak legislation in the near future.

The assessment of sewage sludge management methods requires  an  individual  approach.  When  choosing  treatment sludge management methods, it is necessary to find a compromise between the use of nutrients in the sludge and  the  effective  removal  of  hazardous  components.  It was  found  out  in  the  present  study  that  the  economic viewpoint  should  not  be  the  only  evaluation  criterion. While  direct  exports  of  sewage  sludge  to  agricultural land can be economically beneficial, there are legitimate concerns  about  environmental  and  health  risks.  At  the same time, phosphorus recycling is an important aspect for  sustainable  sewage  sludge  management  techniques, as an extremely important element for fertiliser production, which is in acute shortage in Europe.

Based  on  the  assessment,  the  identified  methods  of sewage sludge management from municipal wastewater treatment plants were divided into groups according to their  suitability.  The  adaptability  scale  was  determined based  on  the  following  criteria:  possibilities  for  removing hazardous substances, recovery of nutrients, cost of technology,  outputs  from  the  technology  and  their  use, energy  demand,  application  in  practice  and  legislation. This evaluation is presented in Table 5.

The methods listed as most appropriate are expensive and not suitable for small treatment plants. The methods identified as most appropriate are most effective, but in large facilities. Supplement with aerobic stabilisation.

In the case of the most suitable methods that were chosen,  there  are  the  thermal  processes  that  were  proven to  be  the  most  effective  for  the  destruction  of  hazardous substances. These processes make it possible to use the energy contained in the organic matter of the sludge while  minimising  the  risks  associated  with  unwanted impurities in the sludge. Among these methods, monoincineration  is  the  most  optimised,  which  at  the  same time ensures the highest phosphorus yield from ash after combustion. Sludge management, such as its direct application to the soil and landfilling, was identified as inappropriate  regarding  to  the  high  risks  of  contamination and  environmental  threat,  or  in  the  case  of  landfilling, moreover,  as  the  hierarchically  most  disadvantageous method of waste disposal without compensatory benefits.

Pyrolysis  and  gasification  are  other  suitable  thermal methods  to  remove  hazardous  substances  contained  in sewage  sludge.  In  these  processes,  a  carbon  residue  is produced,  which  allows  the  recycling  of  phosphorus. However,  it  should  be  noted  that  these  techniques  are not fully established in practice and their research is still ongoing. Composting is considered ineffective in removing  microplastics  and  pharmaceuticals,  while  anaerobic fermentation brings only a partial reduction in the content of pharmaceuticals. In addition, compost and digestate/fugate containing sewage sludge are already limited by EU restrictions on CE certification of fertilizers, and there is a presumption of further tightening of the conditions for the application of such fertilizers to the soil or their strict ban. Although hydrothermal liquefaction is an alternative thermal process, it has a limited potential for phosphorus recycling due to maximising the yield of the liquid fraction-biofuel.

## Conventional methods

Technology description

Anaerobic fermentation

It is a method to stabilise sewage sludge. In the Slovak Republic, anaerobic stabilisation (fermentation) of sludge-methanisation was introduced. The final product is biogas and stabilised sludge (digestate). This process can take place either directly in WWTPs (in medium and large WWTPs for common stabilisation of primary and excess sludge, which are often thickened separately) or in external facilities, most often in biogas plants. Methanation is the most widespread sludge stabilisation process in the EU, using around 40% of the organic matter that is in raw sewage sludge. It is important to note that stabilising sludge does not necessarily mean its sanitation, i.e. pathogenic microorganisms can still occur in over the limit amount even in stabilised sludge, [5] The production of biogas depends primarily on the composition of the supplied sludge, during the stabilisation of which the biogas is released. It contains 60-70% methane-CH 4 , 30-35% carbon dioxide-CO 2  and a small amount of water, sulphate-H S (approx. 0.1%),   N ,   H , ammonia, fatty acids, etc. Thus, 2 2 2 the main components of biogas are carbon dioxide and methane. Both of these gases are relatively difficult to separate from each other, and both are odourless (the smell of biogas is caused by sulphate). The production of biogas also depends on the retention time and temperature, i.e. factors determining the rate of decomposition, because a complete methanisation does not take place in the reactor, where a part of the sludge is continuously discharged [78]. Biogas volumes from sewage sludge can range from 0.75 to 1.12   m  per kg VSS (volatile suspended solids), and the methane concentration is around 60% of the biogas 3

composition [79]

Pretreatments can be used to hydrolyse sludge and consequently improve biogas production, solids removal and sludge quality after anaerobic digestion. According to the nature of the technology, pre-treatment can be classified as thermal, physical (non-thermal), chemical and biological. There are two main thermal treatment/hydrolysis processes according to the applied temperature: high-temperature treatment (100-210 °C) and low-temperature treatment (&lt; 100 °C)

Physical processes for pre-treatment of sewage sludge are processes using high temperature, ultrasound, high pressure, electrical impulse and others, with a predominance of thermal and ultrasonic technologies. Chemical pre-treatments involve the use of chemical reagents to hydrolyse sludge (alkali pretreatment, acid pre-treatment, ozonation. Biological pre-treatment processes aim to intensify hydrolysis during aerobic or anaerobic pre-steps or through the use of enzymes [80]

Processing method

## Conventional methods

Technology description

Mono-incineration

Nowadays thermal processes with sewage sludge can be divided into three basic groups, namely incineration (or so-called mono-incineration where a single type of waste is incinerated, which is the sewage sludge), co-incineration of the sludge with another raw material, fuel or waste, and alternative processes. The

dry matter content and the organic matter content form the main combustible component, and therefore their proportions primarily determine the calorific value of the sludge. It is therefore advisable to dry it before incinerating. In most thermal processes of sewage sludge, they are usually partially dehydrated

(85% of dry matter) or completely dehydrated (&gt; 85% of dry matter) [83]. Dry sewage sludge is characterised by a calorific value in the range from 12 to 20 MJ/

kg, i.e. a calorific value is lower than that of coal (14.6 to 26.7 MJ/kg), but equivalent to, e.g. the calorific value of lignite (11.7 to 15.8 MJ/kg) [84]. However, it should be added that after digestion or stabilisation, the content of organic substances in the sludge decreases and thus its calorific value decreases to values

from approximately 8 to 13 MJ/kg [85]

Mono-incinerators of sewage sludge operate at a temperature in the range from 850 to 950 °C. Temperatures below 850 °C can lead to odour emissions, while temperatures above 950 °C risk ash sintering. The temperature of the combustion process depends on the energy content, the amount of sewage sludge

processed and the amount of combustion air. On the example of German mono-incinerators, it can be stated that they apply sewage sludge either in its raw state or already digested sludge into the process. This can then be additionally drained, semi-dried or dried. In recent years, the stationary fluidised bed has pre-

vailed in mono-incinerators as the most suitable type of sewage sludge combustion system [86]

According to Best Available Techniques (BAT) References Document for Waste Incineration-Industrial Emissions Directive 2010/75/EU (Integrated Pollution

Prevention and Control) [87], the following important factors must be taken into account when incinerating sewage sludge:

- Dry matter content (usually ranges from 10 to 45%-this has a great impact on the combustion process);

- If the sludge is digested or not;

- Lime, limestone and other sludge conditioning components;

- Composition of the sludge as primary, secondary, biosludge, etc.; - Odour problems, especially when dosing the sludge and in storage areas (TWG, TWG Comments on Draft 1 of Waste Incineration BREF, 2003; TWG, TWG Comments on Draft 2 on Waste Incineration BREF, 2004) Options for sludge pre-treatment for mono-incineration are dewatering sludge up to 35% DS; dewatering sludge up to 45% DS; dewatering sludge up to 45%, add a partially drying up to 70% DS; Dewatering sludge up to 45%, add a complete drying up to 90% DS [88]

## Conventional methods

Technology description

Co-incineration

- Sewage sludge can also be co-incinerated with other types of raw materials or waste, i.e. it is used as an admixture of fuel in the combustion process, e.g. (municipal) waste incinerators, power plants, heating plants, etc. For example, in the operation of coal-fired power plants, it was found out that the addition of sewage sludge in the range of up to 5% of weight of charge does not cause any major problems in the process of control or emissions. Sewage sludge can be co-incinerated in power plants incinerating both brown and hard coal. The use of powder fuel or circulating fluidised bed are the main operating systems of the furnaces used for this purpose. In general, only stabilised (i.e. digested) sewage sludge is co-incinerated. Some power plants use only completely dried sludge, in others it is mixed with dewatered sludge and is added back to the incineration process [86]. The optimal proportion of sewage sludge co-incinerated in cement plants is around 7% of weight

Technology description

Landfilling is the placement of waste in a landfill. It is a disposal activity. A landfill is a place with a waste disposal facility where waste is permanently deposited on or in the ground. An inert landfill is a landfill, where the waste producer disposes of their waste at the place of production, as well as a place that has been used for the temporary storage of waste, i.e. for more than one year. A landfill is not considered to be a facility or a place with a facility where waste is stored for the purpose of its preparation before its further transport to a place where it will be treated, recovered or disposed of, if the time of its disposal before its recovery or treatment does not usually exceed three years, or the time of its placement before its disposal does not exceed one year. If the sewage sludge is not used for another suitable purpose, it is disposed of by landfilling

## Alternative methods

Technology description

Reclamation purposes

Reclamation is a type of landscape planning in which anthropogenically altered land is returned to its original state. Its main objective is to achieve a state as similar as possible to the original state and to mitigate environmental impacts by changing physical, chemical or biological properties. The effort is to create conditions for a self-sufficient ecosystem that is biologically and aesthetically acceptable. The most common objects of reclamation are landfills, contaminated areas, quarries, sandpits, and mines. Sludge is mostly used in the creation of reclamation substrates, where it is mixed with waste soil, fly ash from lignite combustion and other waste substances. The goal is to create a mixture that will be a suitable substrate for plant growth. This mixture is created by composting while checking its physical and chemical properties-moisture, nutrient content, pH. The resulting mixture must meet the limits set for the application of waste substances to the soil. These include, e.g. the content of heavy metals, the negative occurrence of pathogenic organisms such as Salmonella and the occurrence of various unfavourable bacteria [95]

The pre-treatment system after reclamation can consist of the following sequence: thickening-anaerobic digestion-dewatering-land application [96]

Technology description

Composting is classified as an aerobic process, in which biological waste is decomposed by microorganisms in the presence of air. Most often, the composting process is provided in the form of heaps, where the material is periodically mechanically rotated to achieve an even distribution of organic materials and sufficient contact with air. It is optimal to keep the process temperature between approx. 55 and 65 °C and the humidity at approx. 35 to 65% so that decomposition takes place at an appropriate rate and pathogenic organisms are destroyed. This process often takes months, depending on the conditions [99] It is desirable to combine sewage sludge from wastewater treatment plants with other waste materials, because it does not usually have an optimal composition for composting on its own (e.g. it can have too high water content). Therefore, in order to produce a suitable material for composting, the sludge is often mixed with wood chips, straw or green waste

Pre-sun-drying (reducing the initial moisture content from 82% to 77.7%) can be one of the methods for pre-treating sewage sludge before composting [100].

Other methods of sludge pre-treatment before composting include enzyme secreting bacterial pre-treatment [101]; microwave [101]; thermal pre-treatment;

alkali pre-treatment [10]

## Alternative methods

Contact dryers

Drying

The heat transfer medium in contact dryers is usually hot oil or steam. The medium is indirectly led to the sludge via contact surfaces. Thus, the principle of contact drying is in heat transfer as in a heat exchanger. Dryers using the principle of contact drying are mainly by type: disc, thin-layer Conventional dryers Conventional dryers include the most drying systems used for sewage sludge. The principle of conventional drying is the direct exposure of sewage sludge to a stream of hot air (heating medium). In the case of use for sewage sludge, the most commonly used types of these dryers are: fluidised, rotary drum, and belt dryer. Other used types include pneumatic, box, tunnel, turbine, spray dryers, etc

Solar dryer

Solar dryers often combine 2 to 3 types of heat transfer: radiation transfer, convection transfer, and contact transfer. The contact transfer is used in the case of the application of additional heating of the bottom of the greenhouse, where thermal energy can be obtained, e.g. from wastewater through a heat pump. From a theoretical point of view, a solar dryer could also be classified as a conventional dryer, because the sludge is basically dried by contact with a stream of hot air, which is driven by fans The performance of a solar dryer is directly proportional to the sum of solar radiation generated by evaporation. In the conditions of the Slovak Republic, 1 MWh per square meter per year can be considered. Residual biomass or ash can be mixed into the loose dried sludge. It is a controlled and organised process for high-quality organic KSP (potassium sulphate) fertilizer. Ash is not an entirely necessary ingredient, but on the other hand, it can have some benefits [103]

## Alternative methods

Technology description

Pyrolysis

Pyrolysis usually treats sewage sludge at temperatures above 350 °C without access to oxygen in order to obtain so-called biochar (pyrolysis coal or solid carbon residue), pyrolysis oil (sometimes referred to as biooil or biofuel) and pyrolysis gas. Pyrolysis oil and gas are mostly used to generate energy. The solid carbon residue is in solid form and can be used in power plants, heating plants or in agriculture The output product of pyrolysis depends on the temperature of the process, where the charring yield decreases as the temperature increases. Therefore, a longer retention time of the charge in a low-temperature reactor with slow heating rates promotes the production of carbon residue, while a shorter or longer retention time at high temperature promotes the production of pyrolysis oil and gas [11] The main product of pyrolysis is generally pyrolysis oil, while most studies in the field of sewage sludge pyrolysis suggest energy applications of pyrolysis oil, mainly for fuel production, less for applications in the field of production of valuable chemical products. Solid carbon residue is usually the main by-product of pyrolysis of sewage sludge with the primary production of liquid-oil Sludge pre-treatments prior to pyrolysis can include aerobic pre-treatment (lower concentration in naphthalene); anaerobic and aerobic digestion (lower overall recovery of semi-volatile compounds compared to sludge without pre-treatment) [105]

## Alternative methods

Technology description

Gasification is a thermal process during which the carbonaceous content of sewage sludge is converted into flammable gas and ash in the presence of a reactive atmosphere, air or steam. Gasification converts mainly organic materials into combustible gas (also referred to as"syngas"), using 20% to 40% of the stoichiometric oxygen needed for perfect combustion, while pyrolysis is a thermochemical reaction that takes place at increased temperatures (500 to 1000 °C) and theoretically in an inert atmosphere without access to oxygen The gasification process uses heat, pressure or water vapour to convert solid organic substances into syngas, which is a mixture of carbon monoxide, hydrogen, and other gases and by-products, i.e. charred coal, or oils and water. The calorific value of syngas from sewage sludge is around 4 MJ/m . Gasification is best 3 if the sludge is dried above 90% of dry matter, but it can also take place with partially dewatered sludge (20 to 40% of dry matter). The gasification process takes place at temperatures of 650 to 900 °C. Typical sewage sludge gasification gas is characterised by a high hydrogen content of 8.89-11.17 (vol. %), CO (6.28-10.77 vol.%),   CH  (1.26-2.09 vol.%),   C S (0.75-1.2 vol.%), carbon dioxide and gasification medium. 7In the first stage of the process, the sewage sludge 4 2 is converted into a flammable lean gas with a temperature of 850-880 °C, which, in addition to nitrogen, consists mainly of hydrogen, methane, carbon monoxide or oxide and long-chain hydrocarbons. In the second stage of the process, hydrocarbons are decomposed by partial oxidation into methane, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen. The resulting synthesis gas is then purified and incinerated, most often in cogeneration, and thus serves for the combined production of electricity and heat [112]

Torrefaction was confirmed as a suitable method for pre-treatment of paper sludge. Torrefaction, also known as mild pyrolysis, is a thermochemical conversion process that introduces a solid feedstock within an elevated temperature oxygen-limited environment and upgrades it to a more energy dense, storable product [113]

## Alternative methods

Technology description

Hydrothermal liquefaction

Hydrothermal liquefaction is a thermal depolymerisation process that is used to convert humid biomass and other macromolecules into petroleum-like substances at moderate temperature and high pressure. This process is also called 'water pyrolysis' [116] It is a process in which biomass undergoes thermochemical decomposition in inert atmosphere and produces a liquid bioraw material at increased temperatures and heating rates with relatively short reaction times [117, 118] Water is used as a reaction medium, which acts both as a solvent and a catalytic agent. The average yield of methyl esters from lipids contained in sewage sludge is 24%, and the total average of saturated fatty acids reaches up to 55%. However, extracting lipids from sludge is expensive and requires a large volume of organic solvent and acidic catalysts [119]

## Innovative methods

Technology description

Bio-electrochemical system

As a new technology, the BES enables sustainable wastewater treatment and energy recovery at the same time. MFC as BES is an environmental and ecological technology that obtains energy through the oxidation of organic substrates and is transformed into electricity using microorganisms as catalysts. They convert organic materials into electrical energy and collectively remove nitrogen and COD by preparing anaerobic and aerobic conditions [123] Microorganisms play a leading role in these systems as they produce electron-rich metabolites, maintain the redox gradient, generate redox mediators, and deliver electrons to the electrode through direct electrons transfer or through a soluble electron transfer mediator with the production of electric current as the end result [124]

## Innovative methods

## Technology description

## Supercritical water oxidation

SCW treatment methods can be divided into SCWG, supercritical water partial oxidation (SCWPO) and SCVO technologies with increasing amounts of oxidants.

Unlike normal water, supercritical water (T &gt; 374.1 °C, P &gt; 22.1 MPa) has a number of unique properties, including a lower dielectric constant, a higher diffusion coefficient, and a lower viscosity. In addition, the solubility of organic matter and gases increases significantly in supercritical water [129] The composition and yield of production gases are affected by many variables, including the properties of the input material such as humidity, process temperature, air-to-biomass ratio, and the presence of catalysts [130] SCWO can be used for treatment of wet organic waste without drying prior to the process since water is the reaction medium. It allows for complete oxidation of organics, essentially without harmful emissions [131]

Innovative methods

Technology description

Biodiesel production

The biodiesel production process using sewage sludge as a feedstock includes lipid extraction and esterification/transesterification or direct esterification/ transesterification in situ. Sludge lipids are mainly derived from the absorbed and/or deposited lipids directly from domestic wastewater, phospholipids in cell membranes, microbial metabolites, and products of ruptured cells. Cellular lipids in sludge include ditriglycerides, triglycerides, phospholipids, monoglycerides, sterols, and free fatty acids. Phospholipids have a percentage of about 24-25% of cells based on dry matter. In addition, fatty acids, sterols and some aliphatic components make up to 36.8% of the composition of dry sludge. The focus of the production process includes the pre-treatment of sewage sludge for more efficient lipid extraction, the extraction of lipids from the sludge itself, the production of biodiesel using extracted lipid or directly from the sludge, and the production of by-products and other value-added products as part of biodiesel production [119] Transesterification is considered the most suitable process. Therefore, it is used in most industries. The low cost, simplicity and reduced viscosity of the oil obtained in this way is suitable for engines and equipment. Transesterification is a process of converting triglyceride and alcohol into fatty acid alkyl ester and glycerol. The process of transesterification can be categorised as a catalytic and non-catalytic process [133] The use of biodiesel has a remarkable impact on reducing global warming by reducing greenhouse gas emissions. It reduces the amount of particulate matter and also reduces smoke due to the presence of free soot [134]. Biodiesel produced from waste products or unwanted materials helps to deal with huge amount of waste that was collected in one way or another, e.g. sewage sludge [135-137]

Technology description

A forward osmosis membrane replaced the traditional three-phase separator of the UASB technology [146]. In forward osmosis, water is transported across a semipermeable membrane from a solution of low osmotic pressure (feed solution), such as wastewater, to a solution of high osmotic pressure (draw solution). The diluted draw solution can later be re-concentrated and clean water can be generated by reverse osmosis or membrane distillation. This way, forward osmosis can be used to extract water from wastewater sources [147] An osmosis membrane bioreactor is an innovative technology that combines traditional biological treatment and forward osmosis (FO) membrane technology and is highly effective for wastewater treatment [146, 148]. This technology has been gaining increasing popularity in wastewater treatment and reclama-

## Conclusion

A key criterion for the management methods of sewage sludge from municipal wastewater treatment plants is the ability to remove hazardous substances and recycle nutrients,  in  particular  phosphorus,  which  is  a  scarce  commodity in the EU for the fertiliser industry. It is sewage sludge that is becoming an important potential source of this  element.  Taking  this  criterion  into  account,  monoincineration appears to be a very suitable technology for treating  sewage  sludge.  Mono-incineration  enables  an effective reduction in the volume of sludge while removing  all undesirable  hazardous  components  (including pathogens,  pharmaceuticals  and  plastics/microplastics, partial  removal  of  volatile  and  semi-volatile  heavy  metals). At the same time, this technology allows for the concentration of phosphorus in the form of ash, which allows for the reuse of this nutrient. It should be noted that, with the exception of phosphorus, other valuable nutrients are lost  during  mono-incineration  that  cannot  be  reused. When comparing mono-incineration with co-incineration  in  terms  of  nutrient  recycling,  co-incineration technology  is  not  able  to  ensure  phosphorus  recycling. In  addition  to  this  negative  aspect,  increased  emissions of  dust  particles  in  the  waste  gas  were  observed  during co-incineration  of  sewage  sludge  in  waste  incineration plants.  The  advantage  of  co-incineration  technology  is in saving fossil fuels and CO2 emissions. However, even without phosphorus content, the ash obtained from coincineration technology is a valuable substitute for input raw material in the cement industry. Pyrolysis and gasification  are  effective  in  terms  of  removing  hazardous components,  but  they  are  complex  technologies  and their economic viability depends on their ability to maximise  efficiency  and  produce  high-value  energy  carriers reaching secondary fuel quality. Otherwise, pyrolysis and gasification  plants  operate  in  the  incinerator  or  waste co-incineration  mode.  From  the  perspective  of  nutrient recycling, the pyrolysis output also forms a carbon residue,  which  is  a  potential  carrier  of  inorganic  fertilizers. However, this advantage is determined by the low accessibility of nutrients to plants and organisms in the soil. For the  above  reasons,  the  technologies  mono-incineration of  sewage sludge; alternative thermal processes (pyrolysis  and  gasification)  and  co-incineration  sewage  sludge were evaluated as the most suitable technologies for the treatment  of  sewage  sludge.  Composting  combines  the advantages  of  removing  unwanted  components  (significantly  reduces  pathogenic  organisms  and  pharmaceuticals) and at the same time, sludge compost can be used as  a  fertilizer  or  soil  conditioner  to  improve  soil  quality. In addition to the above advantages, the composting process also has significant disadvantages (production of gaseous emissions, heavy metals are not immobilised). In addition, a significant disadvantage is the fact that from July  2022,  fertilizers  containing  composts  made  from sludge from municipal wastewater treatment plants cannot obtain CE  certification. Anaerobic  fermentation, like  composting,  has  the  advantage  of  removing  pathogenic components in the digestate. At the same time, this digestate  can  be  used  as  a  fertilizer  or  soil  conditioner to  improve soil  quality,  just  like  composting.  Anaerobic fermentation  has  a  disadvantage  with  composting-it is  not  able  to  ensure  complete  immobilisation  of  heavy metals. Anaerobic fermentation allows for the reduction of  pollutants (pharmaceuticals) in sewage sludge-however, these findings are still in the early stages of research. For  the  above  reasons,  the  composting  and  anaerobic fermentation  technology  was  evaluated  as  less  suitable. Sludge  processing  for  reclamation  purposes  does  not provide either the removal of undesirable substances or the recycling of nutrients. An important advantage of this technology is the low price and simplicity of implementing the technology. When assessing these advantages or disadvantages, this sewage sludge processing technology was  evaluated  as  less  suitable  compared  to  other  technologies.  Drying  is  a  necessary  pre-treatment  step  for several methods of managing sewage sludge, while solar drying  has  significant  limitations  in  Slovak  conditions.

Belt  drying  appears  to  be  the  most  suitable  solution among the evaluated sludge drying methods. Hydrothermal liquefaction has a great advantage over other evaluated thermal sludge management processes-it does not require  sludge  drying,  which  is  energy-intensive.  The process allows the production of biofuel without taking up agricultural land for purposefully grown energy crops. However,  biofuel  requires  major  modifications  to  meet the quality requirements for transport. Another specific advantage of this alternative technology is the potential use of carbon residues for the production of supercapacitors  and  electrodes.  Bio-electrochemical  system  allows the recovery of nutrients and heavy metals from sludge. SCWO provides complete degradation of organic compounds using excess oxidants. However, the disadvantage of both of the above innovative technologies lies in their high  cost.  Although  the  production  of  biodiesel  from sludge as an innovative technology has significant advantages  (the  leaching  toxicity  of  heavy  metals  in  sludge residues meets the relative regulatory values or the reusability of by-products), even in this case the high price is still an important disadvantage. For the above reason, all three innovative technologies were classified as less suitable. Innovative technologies such as thermophilic aerobic  membrane  treatments  and  upflow  anaerobic  sludge osmotic  membrane  bioreactor  are  connected  by  high COD  removal  levels  (more  than  90%).  However,  both technologies  are  still  poorly  investigated  and  therefore the  question  remains  how  effective  these  technologies will  be  in  removing  other  pollutants  (pharmaceuticals and heavy metals) as well as in recycling nutrients (such as  phosphorus).  For  this  reason,  these  two  innovative technologies  were  also  evaluated  as  less  suitable.  However,  it  is  not  excluded  that  in  the  future,  when  taking into account and researching further advantages of these innovative  technologies,  they  will  be  included  among the  most  suitable  technologies  for  sewage  sludge  treatment.  Disposal  of  sewage  sludge  in  landfills  is  not  sustainable  from  an  economic  or  environmental  point  of view. An innovative method of sewage sludge treatment requires  more  attention  from  the  scientific  community  when  implementing  it  into  the  operational  mode. These  methods  are  very  expensive  and  are  not  yet  at the  stage  where  they  can  be  applied  in  the  operational mode.  When choosing sludge  management  methods,  it is  important  to  balance  nutrient  recovery  with  effective removal  of  hazardous  substances.  This  study  showed that economic factors alone should not be the only decision  criterion.  Future  trends  in  sewage  sludge  management  point  to  stricter  limits  on  hazardous  substances, likely  prohibiting land use, and favouring thermal treatment.  Moreover,  as  some  EU  countries  mandate  phosphorus recovery, similar regulations may soon appear in

Slovak law. The research results demonstrate significant potential  for  application  in  various  aspects  of  sewage sludge management and treatment. In addition, a better understanding  of  innovative  techniques  to  reduce  environmental  impacts  was  analysed,  contributing  to  more sustainable waste management practices. As a result, the results of this study are expected to guide future policies and industrial practices and promote a more resilient and environmentally  responsible  approach  to  sewage  sludge treatment.
